title: Three Green Card Categories Just Shut Down for Indians in a Single Month
excerpt: The July 2026 Visa Bulletin has made EB-2 and EB-5 completely unavailable for India while pushing EB-1 further backwards — leaving hundreds of thousands of professionals in limbo until at least October.
body:
The July 2026 Visa Bulletin from the U.S. Department of State has delivered a triple blow to Indian professionals waiting for permanent residency. For the first time in a single bulletin, three employment-based green card categories — EB-2, EB-5 unreserved, and a sharply retrogressed EB-1 — are either completely unavailable or moving backwards for Indian applicants.

The EB-2 category, the most commonly used pathway for Indian tech professionals with advanced degrees, has been marked "Unavailable" for the remainder of fiscal year 2026. No new green cards can be issued in this category for Indians until at least October 1, when the new fiscal year begins and fresh visa numbers are allocated.

EB-5 unreserved — the traditional investor visa category — faces the same fate. And EB-1, typically reserved for multinational executives, outstanding researchers, and individuals with extraordinary ability, has retrogressed to October 15, 2022, a two-month backward slide from December 15, 2022 in June's bulletin. The State Department has warned that EB-1 India could also become unavailable before September 30 if demand continues to outpace supply.

**What 'Unavailable' Actually Means**

When a category is marked "U" in the Visa Bulletin, it means the country's pro-rated annual limit for that category has been exhausted. Unlike ordinary retrogression, where a cutoff date still exists and some applicants can move forward, unavailability is a full stop. No immigrant visas can be issued and no I-485 adjustment of status applications can be approved, regardless of how old the applicant's priority date is.

The one category offering any forward motion is EB-3 India, which advanced slightly to January 1, 2014. But that date is still more than 12 years behind the present, making it impractical for most professionals who filed under EB-2 to downgrade their petitions.

**The Arithmetic Behind the Backlog**

The root cause is a simple mismatch between supply and demand. The per-country cap limits any single nation to approximately 7% of the roughly 140,000 employment-based green cards issued annually. India's pool of skilled professionals in technology, engineering, medicine, research, and management far exceeds that quota, creating a backlog that has swelled to an estimated 1.8 million applicants when dependents are included.

USCIS has confirmed that employment-based applicants must use the Final Action Dates chart — not the more generous Dates for Filing chart — to determine eligibility in July 2026. This effectively tightens the bottleneck further.

**What It Means for Pending Cases**

Applicants with already-pending I-485 applications will not see their cases denied. Their applications remain in queue, and ancillary benefits — Employment Authorization Documents, Advance Parole travel documents, H-1B portability, and AC21 job-change protections — continue to apply during the unavailability window.

But families face difficult decisions. Children approaching the age of 21 could "age out" and lose eligibility as dependents. Professionals weighing job changes must navigate AC21 rules carefully, knowing that any misstep could jeopardize years of waiting.

**The Diaspora Impact**

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals in the United States on H-1B visas, this bulletin underscores the precariousness of their status. Many have lived and worked in America for a decade or more, paid taxes, bought homes, and enrolled children in schools — yet remain tethered to temporary work permits with no clear timeline to permanency.

The July bulletin also arrives as H-1B visa approvals for India's top IT firms dropped 40% in fiscal year 2026, with TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Technologies, and others receiving just 11,041 visas compared to 18,469 the previous year. The Trump administration's tighter visa rules and proposed $100,000 H-1B fee have accelerated the industry's shift toward offshore work and local U.S. hiring.

Immigration attorneys are advising affected Indians to review their cases thoroughly, ensure all EAD and Advance Parole renewals are current, and consider whether EB-1 filings — while also tightening — might offer a faster route than waiting for EB-2 to reopen.

**Looking Ahead**

The next three months will determine whether the freeze holds through the end of the fiscal year. The October 2026 bulletin, which resets annual visa allocations, will be closely watched. But a reset does not erase the backlog — it merely reopens the spigot for another year of rationed supply.

For Indian applicants, the message is stark: the system that attracted the world's best talent is now the system most likely to lose it.

*Sources: U.S. State Department July 2026 Visa Bulletin, Capitol Immigration Law Group, VisaVerge, IndiaWest*
